claims.text: Computed output is not exclusive to aggregation pipelines: find projection accepts aggregation expressions. JAVA-5089 records that this capability started in MongoDB 4.4 and corrects older Java driver documentation that claimed otherwise. (high confidence)

A covered query obtains its filter inputs and result fields entirely from an index without examining collection documents. The same index must contain all required query and returned fields; projection onto indexed fields is therefore necessary but is not alone sufficient to prove coverage. (high confidence)

A compound multikey index can cover a query returning suitable non-array fields, but not the indexed array itself. The multikey documentation also requires that the query omit $elemMatch and satisfy the other coverage requirements. Projecting an array can therefore force document access even when its elements are indexed. (high confidence)

When find sorts and projects the same field, it sorts original values before projection. A pipeline that computes a replacement value before $sort therefore needs a semantic check before being rewritten as find. (low confidence)

Use find(filter, projection) for straightforward field selection; use $project to shape documents at a chosen pipeline stage. Both support inclusion projections and retain _id unless explicitly excluded. (high confidence)

Use server-side projection to return only the fields the application needs. This reduces transferred data and avoids discarding full documents in the application; it does not by itself establish an index-only read. (high confidence)

Coverage requires the same index to supply query fields, internally required fields, and returned fields. Exclude _id when it is absent from that index. A query predicate equating a field to null cannot be covered. (high confidence)

$elemMatch is a find() array projection operator, not a valid aggregation $project expression: the cited Stack Overflow question reports an error when query-projection syntax is placed inside $project. Use an aggregation expression such as $filter; a plain $filter returns every match in input order, so select one match explicitly to preserve $elemMatch's first-match behavior. The cited answer suggests $arrayElemAt. The reproduction does not identify a server version; verify syntax and no-match output on the deployed version. (medium confidence)

Both find() projection and $project include _id by default. Inclusion projections must explicitly suppress it with _id: 0 when it is unwanted. Ordinary field inclusion and exclusion cannot be mixed, except for excluding _id. (high confidence)

If a candidate covering index omits _id, explicitly exclude _id from the result. Otherwise its default inclusion adds a field that index cannot supply. Including _id in the candidate index is an alternative when the result needs it. (high confidence)
Predicates equal to null, such as {field: null} or {field: {$eq: null}}, cannot produce a covered query under the documented coverage rules. (low confidence)

For a projection stage followed by $match, MongoDB can move filters that do not depend on computed projection values before the projection. A filter that depends on a computed field must remain after the computation. Inspect the optimized pipeline rather than assuming the written order is the executed order. (low confidence)

SERVER-135176 reports a covered projection pushdown correctness hazard: after inserting {}, indexing {a:1,b:1}, and projecting {$type:'$b'} after sort/limit, the indexed pipeline returns 'null' instead of 'missing'. The issue is unresolved and lists no affected or fixed versions; this is a reported reproduction, not proof that every deployment is affected. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-22)

Aggregation can also use a covering index for its collection access. Choose between find() and aggregate() for the required semantics, then inspect the actual access plan; the presence of $project neither guarantees nor rules out coverage. (high confidence)

A $project added early solely to reduce fields passed through the pipeline usually does not improve performance: MongoDB automatically prunes fields it can determine are unnecessary. Typically place the output-shaping $project last, while retaining stages whose position is required by computation semantics. (high confidence)

Validate coverage with explain(), preferably executionStats on a representative query that actually returns results. In the documented index-scan plan, a covered read has IXSCAN without an ancestor FETCH; zero totalDocsExamined corroborates the absence of document reads. IXSCAN alone proves index use, not coverage. (high confidence)

The projection argument of find() selects returned fields; the $project aggregation stage shapes each pipeline output document. Both support field inclusion, exclusion, and aggregation expressions that compute or replace field values. A blanket claim that computed projection requires aggregate() is incorrect for the documented find() API. (high confidence)

Studio 3T demonstrates a $project after $lookup to retain selected nested output fields. This is output shaping after a join; it is not evidence that those joined fields can be served from the input collection index alone. (medium confidence)
